items.title: China is mass-producing slop at a scale the world has never seen
items.summary: “A 1960s American retro-futurist city street. A zombie outbreak has just erupted. The city has freshly emerged from battle, wearing the stillness that follows combat. It’s high summer, the sun directly overhead. Cold War, space-age streamlining: rounded, science-fiction domes. Chaos everywhere — wrecked vintage cars, scattered newspapers, blood on the pavement, storefronts from another decade. Zombie corpses litter the street. The leisure of the setting sits in violent contrast to the dead.” The scene is stitched from so many motifs of the old Hollywood zombie picture that any cinephile would feel a flush of recognition. It’s a whimsical love story between a cowboy robot and a mannequin, and the quality of its storytelling and camerawork rivals that of a Netflix or HBO production. The entire three-minute movie is the work of a 28-year-old wedding photographer from a small rural town in Yunnan Province — a man who has never once left China. He goes by Mx-Shell online, and the paragraph you read a moment ago is a slice of the prompt he fed to AI. Today, studios produce micro-dramas the way automotive companies build cars: on an assembly line tuned for sheer volume. Working with Seedance 2.0 — a video generation tool developed by Chinese tech company ByteDance — a handful of asset images, and a script he wrote himself, Mx-Shell produced Zombie Scavenger in just 10 days, spending around 3,000 yuan in token costs (approximately $442). On Douyin, China’s version of TikTok, it has been watched more than 70 million times. Overseas, it has picked up another 12 or 13 million views. PJ Ace, an American AI film producer, went looking for Mx-Shell online to offer him a job. Back in China, the state-run newspaper Wen Wei Po wrote that the creator’s lack of credentials — “the disadvantage that would have shut anyone else out of any other era of filmmaking” — had been erased entirely by AI. He had broken free of the old constraints of technology, capital, and connections to become what the paper called an “army of one.” Everyone I met in China’s nascent AI film industry this past May told me this story with exuberance and starry eyes. He only started learning AI in January! He had no experience before! Mx-Shell’s success had already hardened into the industry’s founding myth — proof that was passed around every dinner table. In the age of AI, anything is possible. Just 3,000 yuan can create a cinematic miracle. The content is made for the thumb and the phone, with plots calibrated to release dopamine on cue. From the outside, China looks like it is leading the world in AI-generated video, cracking Hollywood’s code. Some tech analysts even believe AI micro-dramas could be strengthening China’s soft power (a point I carefully disagree with). Bundle Mx-Shell’s story with the arrival of models like Seedance 2.0 and Kling, a tool developed by Beijing-based tech company Kuaishou, and you might conclude this is another DeepSeek moment, another example of China winning. As a movie lover, Zombie Scavenger made me want to find the second Mx-Shell. But when I set out to write more triumphant stories about China’s success with AI-generated video — about Chinese creators being quicker to embrace AI, about Chinese-developed tools unleashing people’s creativity, and about Chinese AI content winning Westerners’ hearts and minds — I found that Zombie Scavenger and Mx-Shell were an anomaly. The situation I discovered was grim: In China, advanced models, short-video platforms, cloud infrastructure, AI-eager workers, micro-drama studios, and permissive state support have converged to create a monstrous Industrial-Slop Complex, and it has nothing to do with tech diffusion, innovation, or even entertainment. The ubiquitous micro-drama Slop, low-quality digital content that can be produced quickly and in large quantities with AI, was so prevalent in 2025 that Merriam-Webster declared it the word of the year. In China, much of it is built atop the nation’s micro-drama industry, a strange yet profitable juggernaut that churns out cheap, fast-paced videos also known as “short dramas” or “verticals” (because they’re produced in the 9:16 aspect ratio). The content is made for the thumb and the phone, with plots calibrated to release dopamine on cue. Some hail the form as an original Chinese invention — an entertainment current running from China to the West. Today, studios produce micro-dramas the way automotive companies build cars: on an assembly line tuned for sheer volume. Western users can watch them on ReelShort, DramaBox, and FlexTV, Chinese-backed apps built for a single end: making content go viral to eat people’s attention. Every character had the same glossy, overlit skin and stiff gait. A May 2026 report from Yale University argues that Chinese micro-dramas transform “dramaturgy into conversion architecture” — they essentially exploit addictive dynamics to push people to pay. It notes that older serial forms allowed for “ambiguity, scenes that do not convert, moments that deepen character development,” whereas micro-dramas demand instant payoff: “Viewers pay for escalation on schedule, even as the system is designed to defer closure indefinitely.” Micro-dramas can be produced strikingly fast and cheaply, and the production pipeline is often controlled by the platforms themselves, which also collect and use audience data. The line is now being reassembled by AI , which is enabling the micro-drama industry to generate videos at a velocity with no real precedent. The New York Times reported that creators uploaded nearly 50,000 new AI-generated micro-dramas to Douyin in March 2026 alone. That’s almost enough to match the platform’s entire 2025 output. These dramas live in a place with no bearing on human artistic experience. They are monstrous feats of psychological hacking. According to China’s Netcasting Services Association, the nation’s short-drama industry produced about 128,000 micro-dramas in the first quarter of 2026, and 95% of them were fully AI-generated. One industry forecast predicts five million will be produced in 2027 — a hundredfold expansion over 2025’s figure. At a conservative two minutes per drama, 5 million dramas total 10 million minutes of entertainment. It would take someone watching two hours a day roughly 230 years to get through it all. The boom is visceral enough that one AI filmmaker told me that, when she opened a job app, she found more than 400 companies hiring for AI short-drama positions in her area alone. I didn’t have 230 years, but I did have a few days to immerse myself in AI-generated micro-dramas, the majority of which are animated. Instead of whimsical settings like Zombie Scavenger’s “American retro-futurist city,” I discovered countless retellings of just a handful of scripts in just a few genres (neo-traditional Chinese fantasy, time-travel revenge, cut-rate science fiction, etc.), each rendered in a predictable palette with a cheesy plot and over-the-top dialogue. When I moved on to watch contest winners, I found slightly more original storylines, but little visual improvement. Every character had the same glossy, overlit skin and stiff gait. Each setting, whether a Song dynasty court or an intergalactic space station, was overbuilt and overfurnished and way too jelly-like, luxuriant to the point of vertigo. Somewhere around the 15th film, my early excitement about AI-generated cinema was completely gone, replaced by a dizziness and faint nausea from being trapped in the uncanny valley for too long with beings that imitated life but contained none of its friction. Rui Pu The incentives behind the slop I should admit here that I am a techno-optimist. In early 2025, when the AI-generated clip of Sam Altman stealing GPUs went viral, I laughed hard, convinced this would be great. But almost none of the AI micro-dramas being made today were created in pursuit of anything artistic or because someone loved the idea

items.title: How to become a great conversationalist
items.summary: A while back, I was at a party in London where a friend introduced me to an actress who had just been in a big theater production. I was excited to talk with her. Throughout our conversation, she asked brilliant questions, and I enjoyed answering them. She was great at making people feel seen and important. But whenever I asked her something back, with real curiosity about her life, she gave a brief, polite answer and turned the spotlight back on me: “But enough about me, tell me more about you.” You’re probably expecting me to say this made me like her even more. As the conversation went on, though, I started to feel uneasy. She listened well, yet I felt like I was giving a monologue to a great interviewer. By the end, she knew a lot about me, and I knew barely anything about her. On the way home, I kept replaying the conversation, and I realized I might have been doing the exact same thing to other people. I had always been someone who listened more, talked less, and asked a lot of questions. My conversations often felt slightly unbalanced, but I thought I was doing the right thing. I had grown up reading books like How to Win Friends and Influence People , and the main advice in all of them was to listen more than you speak and make the other person feel important. Somewhere along the way, “be a good listener” turned into “don't say too much.” Think about it: If your goal was to get someone to like you, how much of the conversation would you spend speaking? When researchers asked people this question , most said less than half the time, around 41% to 45%. When the goal changed to seeming interesting, the answers flipped to more than half. Most of us seem to believe we’re facing a trade-off: You can be liked, or you can be interesting. It’s the logic behind the popular advice, “It is better to be interested than interesting.” Somewhere along the way, “be a good listener” turned into “don’t say too much.” In a 2022 study , Quinn Hirschi and her colleagues put the trade-off to the test by randomly assigning people to talk for anywhere from 30% to 70% of a conversation with a stranger. Contrary to what people had predicted, the researchers reported that the more participants spoke, the more their conversation partners liked them. The trade-off didn’t show up: The people they liked were also the people they found interesting. An earlier study by Susan Sprecher and her colleagues may help explain why. When one stranger did the talking and the other only listened, the listener ended up liking the talker more than the talker liked them back. Once they swapped roles and both people had shared, the gap disappeared, and liking went up overall. The simplest explanation is that when you talk, you give the other person more to connect to. Sprecher’s listeners felt closer to the talker, and the more the talker had shared, the more similar the listener felt to them. And decades of research show that feeling similar to someone is one of the most reliable routes to liking them. As someone opens up, they become more familiar, you start noticing what you have in common, and liking follows. We clearly like people who talk more, but Hirschi and her colleagues point out that we don’t apply the same logic to ourselves. When it’s our turn to speak, we assume the opposite — that if we want to be liked, we should listen more and let the other person do most of the talking. We find other people’s openness appealing and assume our own will be a burden. The researchers called this the “ reticence bias, ” and they attribute it to a lack of confidence in our own conversational skills. It turns out that most of us are oddly insecure about this skill. In a 2023 study , Christopher Welker and his colleagues asked people to compare themselves with the average person on 20 everyday activities. People rated themselves above average on almost all of them, including reading, cooking, and walking. Holding a good conversation at a dinner party was the only one where they didn’t. When we underrate ourselves as conversationalists, keeping a low profile feels like the safest way to be liked. That’s why “just focus on listening” is such comforting advice: Listening feels a lot safer than putting ourselves out there. None of this is an encouragement to become a conversational narcissist. Taking over with no real listening is a big turn-off for most people. The sweet spot, as Hirschi and her colleagues suggest, is doing both: Great conversationalists talk more and listen well. Talking more gives the other person material to connect with, and good listening makes them feel safe enough to open up. 3 things great conversationalists do 1. Be the first one to go deeper. As Harvard’s Alison Wood Brooks points out , small talk is a perfectly good place to start. The mistake is staying there too long. Research by Michael Kardas and colleagues found that we consistently overestimate how awkward a deeper conversation with a stranger will be and underestimate how much people care about what we share, which creates what the researchers call “a psychological barrier to deeper conversations.” In reality, those conversations felt less awkward than people expected and left them feeling more connected and happier. When you share something real first, you give the other person permission to do the same. You don’t have to reveal your deepest insecurity to be “real”; it can be as simple as bringing up something you’re genuinely excited about. 2. Listen out loud. When we think about listening, we usually picture something passive: staying quiet and letting the other person talk. But good listening involves much more than simply nodding along. Guy Itzchakov and his colleagues define high-quality listening as “empathic, attentive, and nonjudgmental.” In their experiments, people who talked to this kind of listener felt less socially anxious . One way to do this is to ask follow-up questions that build on what the other person just said, which research shows makes people more likable. For example, if someone mentions their grandmother’s cooking, you might ask which of her recipes is their favorite. Researchers also recommend showing you’ve heard someone by reflecting back what they said or returning to something they mentioned earlier — small things like this show people they’ve genuinely been heard. 3. Prepare conversation topics in advance. Most of us go into social events or meetings with a blank mind and hope the conversation will take care of itself. In studies Brooks describes in her 2025 book Talk , 27% of people spent five minutes or more picking an outfit before going somewhere where they expect to have a conversation, but only 18% gave any thought to what they’d talk about. Half expected that thinking up topics in advance would make the conversation less enjoyable, and some worried it would feel forced or scripted. Brooks’s research suggests otherwise: Spending as little as 30 seconds thinking of a few possible topics led to smoother conversations, with fewer awkward gaps and verbal stumbles, and people came away feeling calmer and more self-assured. A few things from your life you’d like to bring up, and a couple of questions you’d love to ask are enough. Both halves of a great conversation Looking back, the actress did everything the classic advice tells us to do. She was curious, she asked brilliant questions, and she made me feel important. But she didn’t quite let me get to know her, and that turned what could have been a real connection into a very polished interview. Listening well is one of the warmest things we can offer someone. But a conversation becomes a connection when both people share something of themselves, and when we hold back, we leave the other person with very little to connect to, however good our questions are. items.title: The ancient environmental archive hidden beneath a northern bog
items.summary: I need to move on and find my field plots, but pausing here has caused my feet to sink. They are now completely buried by peat; only my shins remain visible. I shift my weight from side to side and point my toes to break the suction, releasing a loud squelching retort and sending tiny bubbles to the surface. Walking through boglands requires a marriage of physical and mental strength. My footsteps push deep into soft ground, causing pools of dark cold water to rise over my boots. With no physical boundaries to mark distance, time stretches to match the cadence of bog walking. I pick a careful path, each step punctuated by the slop of rubber boots against sopping moss. The only distraction is the relentless droning of the mosquitoes and black flies encircling my head — a cacophony so loud that I will continue to hear it in my dreams, long after I have returned to firm ground. The threat of breaking through is real. Ankles, knees, sometimes even thighs can be swallowed by the peat, innocent at the surface but becoming sinister with depth. I have learned that the only way to reclaim yourself from the peat is to give in. I have seen those who wage a physical battle against it, their arms pushing down to extract themselves, creating sinkholes of water, which open sideways and fill their clothes with more weight. It is exhausting, and while you struggle, the peat waits patiently, inviting you deeper. Once, walking along a cutline not too far from where I stand now, my field partner became deeply stuck in the peat. She struggled, pushing her arms down until she was nearly waist-deep. Before I could intervene, she impatiently lurched upward and slipped out of her hip-high boots, leaving one buried. As she laughed at her misfortune, I groaned and watched the peat close in around her offering. We tried for hours to extract it, but she ended up walking miles back to our car bootless. Instead, it is better to make peace with the marshland, to give it respect. Suppress the urge to struggle and instead feel the rhythm of the suction as bubbles are pushed up and around your body. Swaying and dancing with peat creates physical space around your limbs that breaks the suction, allowing you, ever so carefully, to rise to the surface and venture on your way, feeling more than a little bit lucky. By the time I get to my field plots, my boots are wet but intact. Rusting metal pins with orange flags frayed by years of weather mark corners of study areas I have monitored for decades. When bogs first form on the landscape, the peat layer — the fundamental base — is thin. With only a shallow veneer of peat separating them from the water table, aquatic moss and other plants flourish. As time passes, peat thickens, lifting the bog surface above the reach of groundwater, known as the regional water table. In this slow rise as bogs mature, their character begins to change. Plants must reach deeper for water, promoting those suited to drier conditions. Low, woody shrubs take hold, from delicate bog rosemary to robust Labrador tea, casting dappled shade on the peat surface as the bog grows more complex. Peat accumulation, surface elevation, and plant species shift together slowly, over millennia. Yet, though I have been monitoring these marked plots for only 20 years, I have witnessed remarkable changes. It is warmer and drier now compared to when I first staked out the plots. The vegetation is different. There is more crusty lichen mixed into the ground vegetation, and the surface peat is dryer and denser. Sphagnum moss is still present, but it looks unhealthy, dry, and bleached out. These are all signs of drought, which has accelerated change at the bog surface, perhaps causing peat accumulation to stop entirely. The next time I visit, a few years from now, the moss may be entirely dead. Such rapid changes, whether as a response to a warming climate or to drainage and agricultural development, are affecting peatlands around the world. Throughout modern history, humans have destroyed bogs, and they continue to do so today. But this bog in the heart of remote northern Saskatchewan tells us that even pristine peatlands far from any farm or city are under threat of rapid change. As I finish making observations from the field plots and close my notebook, I crush a few unlucky mosquitoes between its pages. My notes on the plants and surface peat at this location extend back 20 years, carefully recorded each time I visit this remote place. Sphagnum carpet of an Alaskan bog showing red, green, and yellow mosses. (Credit: Merritt R. Turetsky) But as I stand up, I am aware that beneath my feet is 8,000 years of information laid down in strata. Digging into deep peat is like traveling back in time. Back at the beginning, when the bog first formed, open prairies and tundra dominated Canada, trees were just beginning to demarcate the ultimate sites of today’s great boreal forest, and people around the world were shifting from hunting and gathering to a more agricultural way of living. If we were to dig all the way to the bottom of this bog, we would find the physical existence of that lost landscape, in the remains of the plants and insects that lived and thrived in this very place so long ago. Those remains have now become part of the bog itself, forming peat layers in quiet increments that loft the bog surface up toward the sky ever so slightly, year after year. As peat becomes thicker over many centuries, the accumulation of plant, microbial, and insect fragments — life on the bog surface that resisted the ultimate fate of decomposition and a true return to earth — become a time capsule of change as the bog silently records its impressions for posterity. I reach my hand into the moss, penetrating into peat, pushing straight down until my elbow is buried. Roots poke gently against my fingers, and the entire medium feels wetter and slimier with depth. I grab a handful and pull my arm out of the ground, through the drier epidermis of moss. My skin is now stained almost black, and tiny beads of water cling to my fingers. I cradle the peat in my cupped hand, appreciating all that it represents. This material used to be alive, and I can still make out fragments of moss and sedge parts that grew at the surface when it formed. Those plants drew carbon out of the atmosphere via photosynthesis, and when they died, their biomass and all the carbon contained in it became pages in the bog’s own chronicle. A permafrost bog outside Fairbanks, Alaska, with mossy pools and conifer stands in the background. (Credit: Merritt R. Turetsky) This peat is at the heart of what makes a bog a bog. These are places where a peat layer at least 40 centimeters (about 16 inches) thick has steadily built up. Peat forms when dead plant remnants accumulate faster than microbes can decompose them. This over-abundance of death, and the resultant accumulation of dense, organic layers, is a signature trait of boglands. Other wetlands, like swamps and marshes, remain more balanced on the teeter-totter of life and death: In those places, peat never quite has the chance to form its own crypt. The peat in my hand is not unique to boglands alone. Thin layers of it blanket the surface of many ecosystems, from forests and shrublands to wetlands, and it appears in every terrestrial biome on Earth, from the far north to the tropics. Peat is ubiquitous. In one place, peat might form because microbes are constrained by cold or wet soils; in another, it builds slowly where plant tissues, like dense wood, resist decay. In boglands, many of these peat-forming forces converge, giving rise to thick, spongy layers over time. This usually requires persistent waterlogging, which starves microbes of the oxygen that is essential for the swift breakdown of organic matter. Deprived of oxygen, microbes turn to slower, less efficient chemical reactions. Microbial life persists, but it does so sluggishly, and as a result peat thickens century by centu

items.title: What total darkness reveals about who you really are
items.summary: Could removing light be a key to discovering who you really are? That’s one idea behind dark retreats*, an experience that’s about as close to a complete sensory deprivation chamber as you can get. Participants spend extended periods in total darkness, stripping away the inputs and distractions of everyday life. Andrew Holecek, an interdisciplinary scholar-practitioner in Tibetan Buddhism and other nondual wisdom traditions, believes in the transformative power of dark retreats. Holecek says in today’s society, we’ve become “light junkies,” addicted to the constant distraction of phones, tablets, emails, texts, and everything else competing for our attention. But beneath it all, many feel a sense of emptiness, as if something’s missing and whatever we have is never enough. “We’re so pulled apart from who we are, we’ve lost touch,” Holecek says. “Who you think you are is defined by what you do. Who you really are is revealed when you finally stop doing. The very structure of the self is radically threatened when it’s sent into the dark.” The shock of doing nothing Holecek compares entering the darkness to a cold plunge for the psyche. The shock comes from suddenly doing nothing. At first, it can be intensely boring, even painful. People aren’t able to distract themselves in the usual ways, and about 90% of people contract into a fight, flight, freeze, or fawn response, Holecek says. But as they spend more time in the darkness, something begins to shift. They begin to relax, slow down, and surrender. Then, Holecek says, the mind starts to fall into itself. “In the dark, the mind becomes reality because there’s nothing else,” he says. What emerges in the dark In isolation, the mind may begin to surface experiences and psychological information that have gone unprocessed. “We like to say this is where all the spiders and snakes hang out,” Holecek says. “You receive all this undigested, unprocessed, unmetabolized psychic material, reflections from childhood experiences. It’s going to come up to be, in fact, digested and metabolized in the dark.” The process isn’t easy. People may begin to see who they are and who they aren’t in both exquisite and painful ways. They begin expanding the walls of their Perception Box — the invisible mental box through which each of us experiences the world — Holecek explains. Eventually, he says, the process can go deeper still, reaching what he calls the “primordial contraction.” “The primordial contraction feels like me,” Holecek says. “It feels like the very sense of self, the very thing that I take as a given. Then, you’re going to open it, and that’s where the gold is. You’re forced to make this radical introduction to who you really are.” When nothing becomes everything Entering this environment, Holecek says, can bring about a dissolution of self-structure and identity. People can “drop below the surface structures” of their personal storylines. “The really good news here is nothing really means everything — empty of self means full of others,” Holecek says. In the dark, “it’s not just your eyes that dilate. Your mind dilates. Your heart dilates. Your body dilates. Everything opens. This is the ultimate expansion of all your Perception Boxes.” Of course, no one can stay in the dark forever, and returning to everyday life presents its own challenges, but time spent there can change people’s ability to navigate them. Holecek says people begin to notice the walls of their Perception Boxes contracting again and serving as defense mechanisms against the sensory assault of the conventional world. “It’s the most beautiful and revelatory thing,” Holecek says. “You realize, ‘Oh my gosh, I don’t need to grasp. I don’t need to contract. I can stay open.’” The question then is how to hold onto that openness once the lights come back on. How do you digest and metabolize the experience and incorporate it into everyday life? How do you transform the state into a trait? “That’s the journey,” he says. *Dark retreats can be powerful, intense and disorienting experiences, and they’re not for everyone. This piece is intended to inform and explore, not to provide medical, psychological or mental health advice. We interviewed Andrew Holecek for Perception Box , a Big Think interview series created in partnership with Unlikely Collaborators . As a creative non-profit organization, they’re on a mission to help people challenge their perceptions and expand their thinking. Often that growth can start with just a single unlikely question that makes you rethink your convictions and adjust your vantage point. Watch Holecek’s interview above, and visit Perception Box to see more in this series. This video What total darkness reveals about who you really are is featured on Big Think .

items.title: Current AI is not conscious
items.summary: Is today’s AI conscious? Philosopher Ned Block says no, and he’s not alone in finding the question harder than it looks. In this Mini Philosophy live conversation, Block, Silver Professor of Philosophy at New York University, joins Jonny Thomson to discuss whether consciousness depends on computation alone or requires particular physical processes. Block draws a line between phenomenal consciousness (what an experience feels like) and access consciousness (information broadcast across the mind’s cognitive systems), and explains why AI models may show signs of the second without the first. Along the way, they cover dualism, idealism, and panpsychism, whether consciousness can be studied scientifically at all, how neural networks and backpropagation work, whether AI can be creative, and why Block calls functionalism “hopeless” as a theory of consciousness. They also get into biological naturalism, the case of animal consciousness, Claude’s constitution, and what ethical responsibility we might owe to AI under uncertainty. This video Current AI is not conscious is featured on Big Think .

items.title: What If Breaking Students to Build Them Back Up Only Breaks Them Down?
items.summary: “Obedience to Authority: On Being Broken,” an excerpt from Feels Like Trouble by Helen Betya Rubinstein It was my first class of college, the class I walked across the quad toward on the crisp morning after Labor Day, the empty days of orientation finally over, bell tower clanging out some approximation of a song. Writing the Modern Essay, it was called, which is funny, since Writing the Essay is the name of the course I teach now. We sat in heavy wooden chairs around a tremendous wooden table, all of us on time or early, all of us first-year students, every single one of us the kind of high school student who had wanted to go to Yale and gotten in. We were teacher pleasers and competition winners, elected leaders and admissions-committee-legible achievers, and we believed in the supremacy of our new school—it was why we were here, even if that wasn’t the story we told ourselves, even if some of us had chosen Yale precisely because it wasn’t Harvard. The room was a collective held breath. The walls were paneled in carved wood, the windows too high to see out of, diamond-paned, some of them stained glass. A few minutes after 10 o’clock the professor entered, tall, unsmiling, in a long skirt, her small eyes hard to read. She was pale, face haloed with curly dark hair I’d learn she had a habit of nervously patting. This essay is about her, but I wish it didn’t have to be. Before college, my English teachers had been a motley bunch who made us put our hands on our bellies and practice belting out our voices, or do Surrealist-style automatic writing for 10 minutes of every 50-minute lesson. The high school I’d attended was prestigious—“the best in Louisiana,” it claimed—but it wasn’t rigorous. My chemistry teacher drank wine at his desk and regularly set fire to rings of lighter fluid he’d poured around our chairs. My art teacher built still lifes for us, then spent the rest of the period smoking outside the half-open door. There was one English teacher who sentenced us to interminable months with The Scarlet Letter , and insisted we write according to a formula, but for the most part the department was witchy and weird. I used the medieval Japanese monk Kenko’s “Essays in Idleness” as the model for an essay extolling the glories of the orange, and wrote a play made up of seven colors speaking nonsense, which my classmates performed before the whole school. My advisor, the closest thing I had to a grown-up friend, left handwritten raves at the bottoms of my poems and stories, which she stuffed into my locker and signed with her initials: “EM.” My first college writing professor had the same initials, and would sign her emails and critique letters that way, too. The courses I’d signed up for only reinforced a sinking suspicion that students at Yale were less talented and less interesting than students I’d grown up with. I was walking to the third meeting of that class when my cell phone’s ringer blared and Mom told me a plane had flown into the World Trade Center. The event meant little to me: Still a devoted student of my high school’s norms, I actively ignored anything that might be categorized as “the news.” Our professor showed up late, her face ashen. She offered to talk with us about what had happened and, when we had nothing to say, dismissed us. I padded back across the lawn to my lonely dorm room—I’d been assigned a single I didn’t want—and started work on our first assignment, to write about a time when politics had shown up in our lives. My essay would be about the year David Duke ran for governor, how during third-grade recess I’d stood in a horde of kids shouting “NO DUKES! NO DUKES!” as we watched an airplane write D-U-K-E in the sky. I hadn’t known then that NO DUKES was an echo of NO NUKES, and to be honest I doubt I knew it when I was a freshman at Yale. Months of the KKK Grand Wizard’s campaigning had ingrained the chant as its own thing, memorable as the bumper stickers reading vote for the crook, it’s important , a lesson in choosing the lesser of two evils. To my professor it might have seemed clever that I’d chosen as my topic an election, the baldest possible manifestation of politics showing up in a person’s life. But I was writing about politics in the superficial sense because that was what I thought politics were. She read my playground scene aloud to the class, her approval a rogue flare of welcome amid weeks that had been disorienting and disappointing in ways I was only beginning to let myself admit. The campus was “a medieval Disneyland,” as I would soon put it, the gothic buildings fake paeans to old churches I wanted nothing less than to inhabit. The courses I’d signed up for—introductions to Russian, music theory, and cognitive science—only reinforced a sinking suspicion that students at Yale were less talented and less interesting than students I’d grown up with. What they were, it seemed, was more doggedly devoted to internalizing whatever the professor was saying. In each class there was at least one nervous freshman whose questions turned meetings into dull call-and-response sessions, which dragged on until they were satisfied with their own feats of mirroring. “Imagine the horror of being surrounded by people who look good on paper,” I wrote in the manifesto where I channeled my anger and sorrow. My classmates seemed stymied, small-minded and bland. They “weren’t willing to take risks or think for themselves,” I told my high school advisor in one of the few emails I saved from that dark semester. I wish I’d saved more, because I know that I started going to my professor’s office not only because she and I disagreed about how to revise the work I was turning in—she would never approve of another essay of mine as unreservedly as the first—but also because I’d begun sending her messages criticizing her pedagogy. I would remember this as merely arrogant if I hadn’t practically run toward an opportunity to teach in local schools after that first semester, desperate to undo the damage I felt those months had done. I’d spent the summer before college researching learning styles and brainstorming lesson plans as part of a cohort of “students teaching students,” energized by the force of my convictions about how my eighth-grade English students should learn. In New Haven the following spring, I would encourage kids to write sideways and upside down and with their non-dominant hands, to draw monsters in the margins of their looseleaf pages and read aloud from them proudly, never mind that some of them had begun learning English just weeks before. They were the experts in their own stories—that’s the pedagogy I remember wanting to impart. But I no longer have the messages I sent my professor, just the memory of sobbing in the armchair in her basement office as she handed me a box of Kleenex and explained that she was doing for me as a professor had once done for her: “I’m breaking you to build you.” The office was large, with a rug and a standing lamp whose shade permitted a sallow light. On the wall hung an oversized map of Louisiana. It took several visits for me to register that it was no longer normal to see the geography of my home state arrayed around school. My professor’s proudest publication, it turned out, had been a feature on Cajun Mardi Gras. Where in New Orleans had I lived? she wanted to know. Had I ever been to Mardi Gras in Acadiana myself? Well, I needed to go. She had a fascination with Louisiana, in love with its peculiar foreign rituals. It only made me distrust her more. Those meetings must already have begun by October, when an email from my father advised me to “accept the fact that she is your teacher and you must adopt the writing requirement she imposes. items.title: Einstein’s general relativity equations: explained in plain English
items.summary: Although Albert Einstein is a legendary figure in science for a large number of reasons — including E = mc² , the photoelectric effect, and the notion that the speed of light is a constant for everyone — his most enduring discovery is also the least understood: his theory of gravitation, general relativity . Before Einstein, we thought of gravitation in Newtonian terms: that everything in the Universe that has a mass instantaneously attracts every other mass, dependent on the value of their masses, the gravitational constant, and the square of the distance between them. But Einstein’s conception was entirely different, based on the idea that space and time were unified into a fabric, spacetime, and that the curvature of spacetime told not only matter but also energy how to move within it. This fundamental idea — that matter and energy tells spacetime how to curve, and that curved spacetime, in turn, tells matter and energy how to move — represented a revolutionary new view of how gravitation worked. Put forth in 1915 by Einstein and validated four years later during a total solar eclipse — when the bending of starlight coming from light sources behind the sun agreed with Einstein’s predictions and not Newton’s — general relativity has passed every observational and experimental test we have ever concocted and thrown at it. Yet despite its success over more than 100 years, almost no one understands what the one equation that governs general relativity is actually about. Here, in plain English, is what it truly means. Einstein’s original equation relates spacetime curvature to the stress-energy of a system (top). A cosmological constant term can be added (middle), or equivalently, it can be formulated as dark energy (bottom), another form of energy density contributing to the stress-energy tensor. Credit : University of Tokyo; Kavli IPMU This equation looks pretty simple, in that there are only a few symbols present. But that apparent simplicity fades away as soon as you start asking what those symbols actually mean. Let’s focus on the second version in the figure above: the one that reads G μν + Λg μν = 8πGT μν . The first term, G μν , is known as the Einstein tensor and represents the curvature of space. The second term, Λ , is the cosmological constant: an amount of energy, positive or negative, that is inherent to the fabric of space itself. The third term, g μν , is known as the metric, which mathematically encodes the properties of every point within spacetime. The fourth term, 8πG , is just a product of constants and is known as Einstein’s gravitational constant, the counterpart of Newton’s gravitational constant (G) that most of us are more familiar with. (There’s also a factor of 1/c 4 that gets omitted in this term in the equation, because most physicists set c = 1 when they work with general relativity.) And the fifth term, T μν , is known as the stress-energy tensor, and it describes the local (in the nearby vicinity) energy, momentum, and stress within that spacetime. These five terms, all related to one another through what we call the Einstein field equations, are enough to relate the geometry of spacetime to all the matter and energy within it: the hallmark of general relativity. A mural of the Einstein field equations, with an illustration of light bending around the eclipsed Sun: the key observations that first validated general relativity four years after it was first theoretically put forth: back in 1919. The Einstein tensor is shown decomposed, at left, into the Ricci tensor and Ricci scalar, with the cosmological constant term added in after that. If that constant weren’t included, an expanding (or collapsing) Universe would have been an inevitable consequence. Credit : Vysotsky / Wikimedia Commons You might be wondering what is with all those subscripts — those weird “ μν ” combinations of Greek letters you see at the bottom of the Einstein tensor, the metric, and the stress-energy tensor. Most often, when we write down an equation, we are writing down a scalar equation, that is, an equation that only represents a single equality, where the sum of everything on the left-hand side equals everything on the right. But we can also write down systems of equations and represent them with a single simple formulation that encodes these relationships. E = mc² is a scalar equation because energy ( E ), mass ( m ), and the speed of light ( c ) all have only single, unique values. But Newton’s F = m a is not a single equation but rather three separate equations: F x = ma x for the “ x ” direction, F y = ma y for the “ y ” direction, and F z = ma z for the “ z ” direction, because we live in three spatial dimensions. Instead of a scalar equation, F = m a is an example of a vector equation In general relativity, the fact that we have four dimensions (three space and one time) as well as two subscripts, which physicists know as indices, means that there is not one equation, nor even three or four. Instead, we have each of the four dimensions (t, x, y, z) affecting, or acting on, each of the other four (t, x, y, z) , for a total of 4 × 4 , or 16 , equations. Instead of either a scalar equation or a vector equation, general relativity requires that we go up another level in complexity: to a (rank 2) tensor equation . Instead of an empty, blank, three-dimensional grid, putting a mass down causes what would have been ‘straight’ lines to instead become curved by a specific amount. In general relativity, we treat space and time as continuous, but all forms of energy, including but not limited to mass, contribute to spacetime curvature. In addition, the distances between unbound objects evolve with time, owing to the expansion of the universe. Credit : Christopher Vitale of Networkologies and the Pratt Institute Why would we need so many equations just to describe gravitation, whereas Newton only needed one? Because geometry is a complicated beast, because we are working in four dimensions, and because what happens in one dimension, or even in one location, can propagate outward and affect every location in the universe, if only you allow enough time to pass. Our universe, with three spatial dimensions and one time dimension, means the geometry of our universe can be mathematically treated as a four-dimensional manifold. In Riemannian geometry, where manifolds are not required to be straight and rigid but can be arbitrarily curved, you can break that curvature up into two parts: parts that distort the volume of an object and parts that distort the shape of an object. The “Ricci” component is the volume distorting part, and that plays a role in the Einstein tensor, as the Einstein tensor is made up of the Ricci tensor and the Ricci scalar (which is the sum of the on-diagonal parts of the Ricci tensor), with some constants and the metric thrown in. (The shape distorting part is known as the “Weyl” component, and, counterintuitively enough, plays no role in the Einstein field equations.) When you put down even a single point mass in spacetime, you curve the fabric of spacetime everywhere as a result. The Einstein field equations allow you to relate spacetime curvature to matter and energy, in principle, for any distribution you choose. In the case of an infinitely dense point mass, a black hole results, with an event horizon forming at a distance dependent on the total mass of the black hole. The lowest-mass black holes have the smallest event horizons, but the greatest amount of spatial curvature at those horizons. Credit : JohnsonMartin/Pixabay The Einstein field equations are not just one equation, then, but rather a suite of 16 different equations: one for each of the “ 4 × 4 ” combinations.
